A NATURAL HISTORY OF THE NORTHERN COAST

CHAPTER I

In the year 1847 I first travelled to the northern coast, and it is of
that journey, and of the seasons that followed it, that this volume
gives an account. The reader will find here no argument and no
programme, but only such observations as a patient eye may gather.

The cliffs rise abruptly from the water, and the birds that nest upon
them have been described by earlier writers, though not, I think, with
sufficient attention to their habits in winter. It has often been
argued that they abandon the coast entirely; the evidence suggests
otherwise.

He said, when I put the question to him, that his father had seen them
in December. According to Lindqvist, the same observation was recorded
a century earlier.

CHAPTER II

The village lies in a fold of the hills. Its people have kept records
of the herring since the sixteenth century, and these I was permitted
to examine. For example, the entry for 1712 notes an unusual scarcity,
followed by three years of abundance.

We shall see in a later chapter that this pattern repeats. This book
aims to set down what was observed, and to leave to others the labour
of explanation.

CHAPTER III

Of the interior I can say less. The narrator of an earlier account, one
Petersen, describes a lake of great depth, but I did not find it, and I
am inclined to think he was mistaken, or that the lake has since
drained. Ibid., p. 44.

The winter of 1849 was severe. In the first place the ice came early;
in the second, it stayed. The old woman of the eastern farm told me
that she had never known its like, and she was then eighty years of
age.

CHAPTER IV

I close this volume with a table of measurements, and with the hope
that some future traveller, better equipped than I was, will carry the
work further. The evidence shows that much remains unrecorded.
